question: What predicts yield_pct? Explore how temperature, pressure, and catalyst each relate to yield, how they relate to each other, and produce a variety of chart types.
plain_question: Which of the three things recorded for each production batch - how hot it ran, how much pressure it ran at, and which catalyst was used - goes together with a higher yield, and how do those three relate to each other?
observations: Raw input was a single JSON file holding a flat list of 30 batch records; no wrapper metadata to merge, tidy table = 30 rows x 5 columns (batch_id, temperature, pressure, catalyst, yield_pct), written to records.json.
Outcome framing: 'yield_pct' is present and continuous (28 distinct values, 53.8-80.9%), so this is a correlation/regression story - it was NOT binarised.
No missing values anywhere (0 nulls in 150 cells) and 0 IQR outliers across numeric columns.
temperature: r = 0.90 with yield, univariate R-sq 0.82, slope +0.199 pct-pt per unit.
pressure: r = -0.14 (p = 0.455), univariate R-sq 0.020 - effectively flat.
catalyst: raw group means A 70.2%, B 65.3%, C 72.2% (ANOVA p = 0.080), but group mean temperature is A 203, B 179, C 200.

Model choice: OLS on a continuous outcome (logistic/Poisson would not apply); catalyst entered as a FIXED effect rather than a random effect because it has only 3 levels, too few to identify a variance component. Batch ids are unique, so there are no repeated measures.
Full model R-sq 0.862 (adj 0.840), residual SD 2.76 pct-pt, max VIF 1.56, Shapiro p 0.785, Breusch-Pagan p 0.166.

Functional form: a squared temperature term and a temperaturexpressure interaction were each fitted (tables/functional_form_checks.csv); the best of them raised R-squared by only 0.005 over the additive model, so the straight-line description was kept rather than assumed.

takeaways.title: temperature is the dominant correlate of yield_pct: r = 0.90 (95% CI 0.81 to 0.95, n=30), univariate R-sq = 0.82, slope +0.199 pct-pt per unit (adjusted +0.190 [+0.154, +0.226]).
takeaways.plain_title: Running a batch hotter is by far the best predictor of a good yield: every extra 10 degrees goes with about 2.0 more percentage points of yield, and temperature alone accounts for roughly 82% of the difference between batches.
takeaways.analysis: Across 30 batches the temperature-yield_pct correlation is 0.90 (Spearman 0.87, so it is not driven by a couple of extreme points), and temperature on its own explains 82% of the yield spread. The adjusted slope is +0.190 percentage points of yield per unit of temperature with a 95% interval of [+0.154, +0.226], which excludes zero. Every other measured factor is far behind on the ranked association chart.
takeaways.caveat: Descriptive association only. These are observational batch records, not a designed experiment, so no causal reading is supported; the relationship is only characterised inside the observed temperature range (155 to 248).

takeaways.title: The binned mean-yield_pct curve rises monotonically from 62.3% (155-164, n=6) to 78.0% (234-248, n=6), a 15.7 pct-pt span with no plateau or turning point.
takeaways.plain_title: Average yield climbs steadily across the whole temperature range - from about 62% in the coolest batches to about 78% in the hottest - with no sign of levelling off or a sweet spot in between.
takeaways.analysis: Equal-count temperature bands give mean yields of 62.3% (155-164, n=6), 63.8% (164-179, n=6), 68.7% (179-203, n=6), 74.3% (203-234, n=6), 78.0% (234-248, n=6). The ordering is strictly increasing, which is why a straight-line summary is a fair description here rather than an assumption imposed on the data.
takeaways.caveat: Bands hold 5-7 batches each, so band-to-band wobble of a point or two is within noise; the data cannot say what happens outside the observed temperature range.

takeaways.title: pressure shows no material association with yield_pct: r = -0.14 (p = 0.455), univariate R-sq = 0.020; adjusted slope -0.81 pct-pt per unit with 95% CI [-2.14, +0.51] spanning zero.
takeaways.plain_title: Pressure looks essentially unrelated to yield - batches run at high and low pressure end up with much the same yields, and the small downward tilt that does appear is well within what random variation would produce.
takeaways.analysis: The marginal correlation between pressure and yield_pct is -0.14, explaining under 2% of yield variation, and the binned curve is flat rather than sloped. Adding pressure to the model changes explained variance by only 0.009, and its added-variable panel shows no residual trend. It is the clearest negative result in this dataset.
takeaways.caveat: Absence of an association over the observed pressure range (3.03 to 5.99) is not evidence that pressure never matters; a wider range, or an interaction, could behave differently, and n=30 limits sensitivity to small effects.

takeaways.title: The raw catalyst gap (C 72.2% vs B 65.3%, one-way ANOVA p = 0.080) largely tracks a 21-unit temperature imbalance between groups; adjusted for temperature the largest catalyst coefficient is 2.07 pct-pt with intervals spanning zero (delta R-sq = 0.032).
takeaways.plain_title: Catalyst B looks like the weakest performer on raw numbers (65.3% vs 72.2% for catalyst C), but its batches were also run about 21 degrees cooler - once you compare batches run at similar temperatures the catalyst gap nearly disappears.
takeaways.analysis: Group means are A 70.2% (n=11), B 65.3% (n=9), C 72.2% (n=10), but mean temperature per group is A 203, B 179, C 200 - the low-yield group is also the cool-running group, and the ECDF shows the whole distribution is shifted, not just the mean. On temperature-adjusted values the violins line up and the catalyst terms add only 0.032 to R-squared.
takeaways.caveat: This describes an imbalance in the recorded conditions, not a demonstration that the catalysts are equivalent. With 9-11 batches per group and overlapping but unequal temperature ranges, a genuine moderate catalyst effect could still be hidden.

takeaways.title: Nested models: temperature-only R-sq = 0.818 vs full model R-sq = 0.862 (adj 0.840); pressure and catalyst together add 0.044.
takeaways.plain_title: Almost everything the data can explain about yield comes from temperature alone: adding pressure and catalyst on top lifts the explained share only from about 82% to 86%.
takeaways.analysis: An ordinary least-squares fit of yield_pct on temperature, pressure plus catalyst reaches R-squared 0.862 with residual SD 2.76 percentage points, versus 0.818 for temperature alone. The predicted-vs-observed calibration line tracks the diagonal across the range, and residual checks are unremarkable (Shapiro p = 0.79, Breusch-Pagan p = 0.17, 2 batches above the Cook's-distance 4/n mark).
takeaways.caveat: R-squared is measured on the same 30 rows used to fit, so it is optimistic as a prediction estimate; no held-out split was evaluated here.

takeaways.title: temperature and pressure are near-orthogonal (r = -0.03; max VIF = 1.56), so numeric coefficients are stable; the only structured imbalance is catalyst-by-temperature.
takeaways.plain_title: Temperature and pressure were dialled independently of each other - knowing one tells you almost nothing about the other - so neither is standing in for the other. The only pairing that is genuinely tangled together here is which catalyst was used and how hot that batch was run.
takeaways.analysis: The correlation heatmap shows temperature-pressure at -0.03, and all variance-inflation factors are at or below 1.56, far under the usual concern level of 5. Marginal and adjusted slopes therefore agree closely for both numeric factors, which is why the temperature result barely moves when other terms enter the model.
takeaways.caveat: Low collinearity among the measured factors says nothing about unmeasured factors (feedstock, operator, equipment, time order) that are not in this table at all.

takeaways.title: Residual SD is 2.76 pct-pt and 14% of yield_pct variance is unexplained by temperature, pressure + catalyst; the data has no time, operator or feedstock column to probe it.
takeaways.plain_title: Even after accounting for every recorded setting, individual batches still land about 2.8 percentage points either side of what the settings alone would suggest - so roughly 14% of the batch-to-batch variation is coming from something this table does not record.
takeaways.analysis: Observed yields span 53.8-80.9% around a mean of 69.4%. The fitted model leaves a residual SD of 2.76 percentage points with no visible pattern against predicted values, i.e. the leftover variation looks like unstructured batch noise rather than a missed curve in the recorded factors. The tidy table has only 5 columns (batch_id, temperature, pressure, catalyst, yield_pct), so no further covariate is available to examine.
takeaways.caveat: Unexplained variance is not evidence of randomness - it can equally reflect variables that were never recorded in this extract.

hypotheses.statement: The apparent catalyst B yield deficit (65.3% vs C 72.2%) is not a chemical property of B but an artefact of non-random assignment — B is preferentially used on cooler runs (group mean 179 vs 200–203), so its "penalty" is inherited temperature and should shrink to under ~2 pct-pt when temperature is matched by design.
hypotheses.plain_statement: Catalyst B looks worse only because it happened to be used on the cooler batches; if all three catalysts were run at the same temperature, they would perform about the same.
hypotheses.basis: Catalyst takeaway (raw gap p = 0.080 but temperature-adjusted effect ≤ 2.07 pct-pt with intervals spanning zero, delta R-sq 0.032); the catalyst-by-temperature imbalance flagged as the only structured imbalance in the design.
hypotheses.test_design: Run a balanced experiment in which each catalyst is used at the same set of temperatures (e.g. 170, 200, 230, several batches each); the claim survives if the catalyst gap collapses to within a couple of percentage points at every temperature level, and is refuted if B stays roughly 7 points below C even at matched temperature — or if B underperforms specifically at high temperature, which would instead point to a real catalyst-by-heat interaction.

hypotheses.statement: Pressure is flat (r = -0.14, added R-sq 0.009) because the plant already operates entirely above the pressure threshold at which the reaction saturates, so the recorded pressure spread is post-saturation control jitter rather than a lever; the "hot and low-pressure" interaction should therefore also be null, and pressure sensitivity should only reappear below the operated range.
hypotheses.plain_statement: Pressure does not show up as important because the process is already run at more than enough pressure for the reaction — turning that dial within its normal range does nothing, and it would only start to matter if pressure were dropped well below what the plant currently uses.
hypotheses.basis: Pressure takeaway (r = -0.14, p = 0.455, adjusted slope CI spanning zero, flat binned curve, no residual trend); the near-orthogonality of temperature and pressure (r = -0.03) which rules out pressure being masked by temperature; the "hot and low-pressure combination" interaction candidate.
hypotheses.test_design: Deliberately extend the pressure range downward (batches at, say, 50% and 25% of the current minimum) at fixed temperature; the claim survives if yield is unchanged across the current range but falls off sharply below it, and is refuted if yield stays flat even at much lower pressure (pressure is simply irrelevant) or if a temperature × pressure interaction term becomes significant within the existing range.

dashboard_storyboard.title: Problem Setting
dashboard_storyboard.summary: 30 production batches, each with three recorded settings - temperature, pressure and catalyst - and a continuous outcome, yield_pct (mean 69.4%, range 53.8-80.9%). The question is which of those settings tracks yield, how they relate to one another, and whether any apparent group effect survives the others. There is no pass/fail label in this data, so the analysis is framed as correlation and regression, not FAIL vs PASS.
items: Data: one JSON file, flat list of 30 batch records, no missing values, parsed into a tidy 30x5 table (records.json).
Outcome: yield_pct, continuous - deliberately NOT binarised into pass/fail.
Factors examined: temperature, pressure (numeric) and catalyst (3 levels, 9-11 batches each).

Method: variable EDA -> per-factor association with effect sizes and intervals -> conditioning check for confounding -> marginal screening -> ordinary least squares with catalyst as a fixed effect -> collinearity, residual and calibration diagnostics.
Everything reported is descriptive association; nothing here is a causal or confirmed result.

claims.text: temperature is the strongest measured correlate of yield_pct in these 30 batches (r = 0.90, 95% CI 0.81 to 0.95).
claims.interpretation: The leading candidate driver for any downstream confirmatory work.
claims.do_not_infer: Not causal and not confirmed; a single observational batch set cannot separate temperature from anything that co-varies with it.

claims.text: pressure shows no material association with yield_pct over the observed range (r = -0.14, adjusted 95% CI [-2.14, +0.51] pct-pt per unit).
claims.interpretation: A negative screening result for pressure at this sample size and range.
claims.do_not_infer: Not evidence of no effect; n=30 gives limited power and the observed range is narrow.

claims.text: The unadjusted catalyst yield ordering coincides with a 21-unit difference in mean temperature between the same groups, and catalyst adds only 0.032 to R-squared once temperature is in the model.
claims.interpretation: A condition-imbalance pattern that any downstream comparison of catalysts must handle.
claims.do_not_infer: Does not establish that the catalysts are equivalent, nor that temperature explains the gap.

caveats: n = 30 batches. Every interval is wide at this size; group-level statements rest on 9-11 batches each.
Observational batch records with no randomisation and no time/operator/feedstock columns - associations here cannot be separated from unrecorded factors.
catalyst groups were not run over the same temperature range, so catalyst and temperature are entangled by design of the data, not by choice of analysis.
All R-squared and correlation figures are in-sample on the same 30 rows used for fitting; no held-out split was evaluated.
Relationships are only characterised inside the observed ranges (temperature 155-248, pressure 3.03-5.99).
Per-catalyst correlation slopes were computed (stratified_correlations table) but not charted, since 9-11 batches per group make a per-group trend line unstable.
No binary FAIL/PASS split exists in this data and none was invented; class-balance and fail-rate visuals were deliberately skipped.
critique: Double-dipping: the same 30 rows were used for screening, model fitting and the reported R-squared, so effect sizes are optimistic. A held-out or cross-validated estimate would be lower.

The catalyst-vs-temperature imbalance is a textbook confounding structure; the 'adjusted' catalyst panel relies on the linear temperature adjustment being right, and with partly non-overlapping ranges that adjustment is doing extrapolation for part of each group.
No leakage risk was identified - none of the predictors is a re-measurement of yield - but this was checked by inspection of column semantics only, not by any provenance record.
With 3 catalyst levels a mixed-effects model was deliberately not fitted; if more catalysts existed, a random intercept would be the better choice and conclusions about group spread could shift.
Multiple comparisons were not adjusted for: several tests were run across factors, so borderline p-values (e.g. the raw catalyst ANOVA) should not be read as a threshold decision.
Charts using equal-count bins can visually exaggerate a trend when bins are uneven in width; the raw scatter is provided alongside precisely so the reader can check that.
recommended_confirmatory_tests: On a held-out batch set, regress yield_pct on temperature and report the slope with a 95% interval; check whether it lands near +0.190 pct-pt per unit.
Compare catalyst groups within narrow temperature strata (or with temperature as a covariate) on new batches, so the catalyst comparison is not carried by the temperature imbalance seen here.
Test the temperature x pressure interaction explicitly on new data; it was small here (delta R-sq below 0.01) but n=30 gives little power to detect it.
Evaluate the temperature-only model against the full model by cross-validated prediction error, to see whether the extra terms earn their place out of sample.
Extend the recorded pressure range and re-test - the current flat result only covers 3.03-5.99.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Exploratory analysis: what predicts yield_pct in the reactor-batch dataset?

Self-contained. Reads whatever is under raw_input/, builds ONE tidy table,
writes records.json, tables/*.csv (host-rendered chart data) and figures/*.png
(rich distribution-first figures), then prints EXPLORATORY_RESULT_JSON.

Method follows the outcome-driver-analysis skill, adapted to a CONTINUOUS
outcome (linear regression rather than logistic):
  1. intake / structure       2. explanatory-variable EDA
  3. per-variable vs outcome  4. marginal screening
  5. justified model          6. fit diagnostics (VIF, residuals, calibration)
  7. result visuals           8. descriptive narrative

Everything reported is DESCRIPTIVE. No causal claims, no verdicts.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import os
import sys
import warnings
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

RAW_DIR = Path("raw_input")
TABLES = Path("tables")
FIGS = Path("figures")
TABLES.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
FIGS.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

TARGET = "yield_pct"  # caller-specified outcome column
RECORD_KEYS = ("cases", "results", "rows", "items", "data", "examples", "samples", "records", "batches")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. LOAD -> ONE TIDY TABLE  (shape is not assumed; it is inspected)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
def _rows_from_obj(obj, meta=None, src=""):
    """Recursively turn an arbitrary JSON object into a list of flat row dicts."""
    meta = dict(meta or {})
    if isinstance(obj, list):
        if obj and all(isinstance(x, dict) for x in obj):
            return [{**meta, **_flatten(x)} for x in obj]
        return []
    if isinstance(obj, dict):
        # dict of scalar metadata + a list of per-case records under some key
        list_keys = [k for k, v in obj.items() if isinstance(v, list) and v and all(isinstance(i, dict) for i in v)]
        scalar_meta = {k: v for k, v in obj.items() if not isinstance(v, (list, dict))}
        if list_keys:
            preferred = [k for k in RECORD_KEYS if k in list_keys] or list_keys
            out = []
            for k in preferred:
                child_meta = {**meta, **scalar_meta}
                if len(preferred) > 1:
                    child_meta["_record_group"] = k
                out.extend([{**child_meta, **_flatten(r)} for r in obj[k]])
            return out
        # dict-of-dicts keyed by id
        if obj and all(isinstance(v, dict) for v in obj.values()):
            return [{**meta, "_key": k, **_flatten(v)} for k, v in obj.items()]
        return [{**meta, **_flatten(obj)}] if obj else []
    return []


def _flatten(d, prefix=""):
    """One level of dict flattening; lists of scalars become a joined string."""
    out = {}
    for k, v in d.items():
        key = f"{prefix}{k}"
        if isinstance(v, dict):
            out.update(_flatten(v, prefix=f"{key}_"))
        elif isinstance(v, list):
            if all(not isinstance(i, (dict, list)) for i in v):
                out[key] = ", ".join(map(str, v))
            else:
                out[key] = json.dumps(v)[:200]
        else:
            out[key] = v
    return out


def load_tidy() -> pd.DataFrame:
    files = sorted(p for p in RAW_DIR.rglob("*") if p.is_file() and p.suffix.lower() in {".json", ".jsonl", ".ndjson", ".csv"})
    if not files:
        raise SystemExit("no readable files under raw_input/")

    # A browser-workbench bundle would carry records.json; prefer it when present.
    normalized = [p for p in files if p.name == "records.json"]
    if normalized:
        files = normalized + [p for p in files if p not in normalized and p.name != "records.json"]

    rows = []
    for path in files:
        text = path.read_text(errors="replace").strip()
        if not text:
            continue
        meta = {} if len(files) == 1 else {"source_file": path.name}
        if path.suffix.lower() == ".csv":
            rows.extend(pd.read_csv(path).to_dict("records"))
            continue
        try:
            rows.extend(_rows_from_obj(json.loads(text), meta=meta, src=path.name))
        except json.JSONDecodeError:  # JSONL / NDJSON
            for line in text.splitlines():
                line = line.strip()
                if not line:
                    continue
                try:
                    rows.extend(_rows_from_obj(json.loads(line), meta=meta, src=path.name))
                except json.JSONDecodeError:

        if normalized and path.name == "records.json":
            break  # normalized rows are authoritative

    df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    # numeric coercion for object columns that are really numbers
    for c in df.columns:

            conv = pd.to_numeric(df[c], errors="coerce")
            if conv.notna().mean() > 0.9 and conv.notna().sum() > 0:

def fisher_ci(r, n, alpha=0.05):
    if n < 4 or not np.isfinite(r) or abs(r) >= 1:
        return (np.nan, np.nan)
    z = np.arctanh(r)
    se = 1.0 / np.sqrt(n - 3)
    crit = stats.norm.ppf(1 - alpha / 2)
    return tuple(np.tanh([z - crit * se, z + crit * se]))


def human_bins(series, q=5):
    """Quantile bins with human labels like '155-174' (never raw pandas.cut edges)."""
    qs = min(q, max(2, series.nunique() // 3))
    edges = np.unique(np.quantile(series.dropna(), np.linspace(0, 1, qs + 1)))
    if len(edges) < 3:
        edges = np.linspace(series.min(), series.max(), 4)
    idx = np.clip(np.digitize(series, edges[1:-1], right=True), 0, len(edges) - 2)
    labels = [f"{edges[i]:.0f}-{edges[i+1]:.0f}" if edges[-1] > 20 else f"{edges[i]:.1f}-{edges[i+1]:.1f}"
              for i in range(len(edges) - 1)]
    centers = [(edges[i] + edges[i + 1]) / 2 for i in range(len(edges) - 1)]
    return pd.Series([labels[i] for i in idx], index=series.index), np.array(labels), np.array(centers)

def pretty(term):
    """Turn a patsy term (C(Q('catalyst'))[T.B]) into a human label (catalyst = B)."""
    if term == "Intercept":
        return term
    m = re.match(r"C\(Q\('([^']+)'\)\)\[T\.(.+)\]$", term)
    if m:
        return f"{m.group(1)} = {m.group(2)}"
    m = re.match(r"Q\('([^']+)'\)$", term)
    if m:
        return m.group(1)
    return re.sub(r"[CQ]?\(?'?|'?\)?", "", term)
